notes.definition: An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions in the lattice.
explanation: An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions. The positive and negative ions are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern called a giant ionic lattice. The word giant means that the structure continues in all directions and contains a huge number of ions; it is not made of separate molecules. Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. These forces act in all directions in the lattice, so each ion is attracted to all of the oppositely charged ions around it.

You need to know the structure of sodium chloride. In solid sodium chloride, each sodium ion (Na⁺) is surrounded by chloride ions (Cl⁻), and each chloride ion is surrounded by sodium ions, in a cubic arrangement. There are equal numbers of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, which is why the formula is NaCl. The chloride ions are larger than the sodium ions. You do not need to learn the structures of other ionic compounds, but you should be able to recognise that a compound is ionic from a diagram that shows charged particles arranged in a regular lattice.

Ionic structures can be represented in several ways, and each has limitations. A dot and cross diagram shows how the ions formed and where the electrons came from, but it does not show how the ions are arranged in the lattice or their relative sizes, and it suggests the compound is made of separate pairs of ions. A ball and stick model shows the three-dimensional arrangement of the ions, but the sticks suggest physical bonds between pairs of ions, whereas the attraction acts in all directions. It also leaves large gaps between ions, whereas in reality the ions are packed closely together.

A two-dimensional diagram shows the pattern of ions in one layer only, so it does not show the three-dimensional structure. A three-dimensional space-filling model shows how the ions are packed and their relative sizes, but you can only see the ions on the outside, so the arrangement inside is hidden. All of these diagrams show only a tiny part of the lattice: a real crystal contains billions of ions. None of the models shows the electrostatic forces themselves.

You can work out the empirical formula of an ionic compound from a model or diagram. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of the ions. Count the ions in a repeating section of the diagram, or count the positive and negative ions and simplify the ratio. For example, if a diagram shows one positive ion for every two negative ions, the formula is MX₂. You can check this with the charges: the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge, so a 2+ ion needs two 1− ions.
keyFacts: An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions (a giant ionic lattice).
Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
The forces act in all directions in the lattice.
Sodium chloride: each Na⁺ is surrounded by Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by Na⁺ ions, in a regular cubic arrangement.
There are no molecules in an ionic compound.
Dot and cross diagrams do not show the arrangement of ions in the lattice.
Ball and stick models wrongly suggest bonds are sticks and that there are gaps between ions.
2D diagrams show only one layer; 3D space-filling models hide the inner ions.
Empirical formula = simplest whole-number ratio of ions, found by counting ions in a diagram.

keyTerms.definition: A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of a very large number of oppositely charged ions.
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms or ions of each element in a compound.
A model in which ions or atoms are shown as balls joined by sticks to show their positions in a structure.
A three-dimensional model in which the spheres touch, showing the relative sizes and close packing of particles.
A regular repeating arrangement of particles in three dimensions.

workedExamples.title: Empirical formula from a diagram
workedExamples.question: A diagram of part of an ionic lattice shows 8 calcium ions and 16 fluoride ions. Work out the empirical formula of calcium fluoride.
steps: Write the ratio of ions: Ca : F = 8 : 16.
Divide both numbers by the smaller number (8): 1 : 2.
Check charges: Ca²⁺ and F⁻, so 1 × (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0.

workedExamples.title: Recognising an ionic structure
workedExamples.question: A diagram shows a regular three-dimensional arrangement of particles labelled with + and − charges, alternating throughout the structure. Deduce the type of structure and explain your answer.
steps: The particles carry charges, so they are ions, not atoms or molecules.
Positive and negative ions alternate in a regular repeating pattern in three dimensions.
This is a giant lattice held by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
workedExamples.answer: A giant ionic lattice (an ionic compound), because it is a regular arrangement of oppositely charged ions.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a model
workedExamples.question: Give one strength and one limitation of a ball and stick model of sodium chloride.
steps: Strength: it shows the three-dimensional arrangement, with each ion surrounded by oppositely charged ions.
Limitation: the sticks suggest bonds are physical links in fixed directions between pairs of ions, and the gaps between the ions are much larger than in reality.
workedExamples.answer: Shows the 3D arrangement of ions; but sticks are not real and ions are actually closely packed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sodium chloride is made of NaCl molecules.
misconceptions.right: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice. NaCl is the ratio of ions (1 : 1), not a molecule.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think each ion is bonded to only one ion of opposite charge (its 'partner' from electron transfer).
misconceptions.right: Each ion is attracted to all of the oppositely charged ions around it, because electrostatic forces act in all directions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the sticks in a ball and stick model are real bonds.
misconceptions.right: The sticks only show the positions of the ions; the attraction is not a physical link and acts in all directions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the forces in ionic compounds are weak because salt dissolves in water.
misconceptions.right: The electrostatic forces are strong; dissolving involves water molecules attracting the ions, which is a separate process.

realWorld: Salt crystals are cube-shaped because the ions in sodium chloride are arranged in a cubic lattice.
Chemists use X-ray crystallography to work out the arrangement of ions in a crystal, which is how the structure of sodium chloride was first confirmed.
Rock salt (halite) mined in Cheshire is a giant ionic lattice of sodium chloride used for gritting roads.
examTips: Always use the phrase 'strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions' and add 'in all directions' when describing the lattice.
Never call an ionic compound a molecule, and never use the words 'intermolecular forces' for ionic compounds.
For limitation questions, say what the model shows AND what it fails to show (for example 'ball and stick shows the 3D arrangement but the sticks are not real bonds').
When finding an empirical formula from a diagram, count carefully, then simplify the ratio and check that the charges balance.
summary: Ionic compounds are giant structures of ions.
They are held by strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions.
In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by Na⁺ ions.
Every type of diagram (dot and cross, ball and stick, 2D, 3D) has limitations.
The empirical formula is the simplest ratio of ions, which you can find by counting ions in a diagram.

questions.question: What type of structure does sodium chloride have?
options: Simple molecular
Giant covalent
Giant ionic lattice
Metallic
markScheme: 1 mark: Giant ionic lattice
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions arranged in a giant ionic lattice. It does not contain molecules.

questions.question: What holds the ions together in an ionic compound?
options: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
Shared pairs of electrons
Weak intermolecular forces
Delocalised electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds are held by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Shared pairs are covalent bonds and delocalised electrons are found in metals.

questions.question: In which directions do the electrostatic forces act in an ionic lattice?
options: Only between pairs of ions
Only in two dimensions
Only vertically
In all directions
markScheme: 1 mark: In all directions
questions.explanation: Each ion attracts all the oppositely charged ions around it, so the forces act in all directions.

questions.question: In a crystal of sodium chloride, which ions surround each sodium ion?
options: Sodium ions
Chloride ions
Chlorine molecules
Sodium atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: Chloride ions
questions.explanation: Each Na⁺ is surrounded by Cl⁻ ions, and each Cl⁻ by Na⁺ ions. Ions of the same charge would repel.

questions.question: A diagram of part of an ionic lattice shows 6 magnesium ions and 12 bromide ions. What is the empirical formula?
options: Mg₂Br
Mg₆Br₁₂
MgBr
MgBr₂
markScheme: 1 mark: MgBr₂
questions.explanation: Ratio 6 : 12 simplifies to 1 : 2. Check: Mg²⁺ and two Br⁻ give zero overall charge. Mg₆Br₁₂ is not the simplest ratio.

questions.question: Which is a limitation of a ball and stick model of an ionic compound?
options: It shows the ions in three dimensions.
It shows that each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions.
It suggests there are large gaps between the ions.
It shows the regular pattern of the ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: It suggests there are large gaps between the ions.
questions.explanation: In reality the ions are closely packed; the model exaggerates the spaces. The other options are strengths of the model.

questions.question: Which is a limitation of a dot and cross diagram for sodium chloride?
options: It does not show the arrangement of ions in the lattice.
It shows the charges on the ions.
It shows where the electrons came from.
It shows that sodium loses an electron.
markScheme: 1 mark: It does not show the arrangement of ions in the lattice.
questions.explanation: Dot and cross diagrams show electron transfer and charges well, but not how ions are arranged in the giant structure.

questions.question: Which description of a substance shows that it is an ionic compound?
options: A regular lattice of positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons
A regular lattice of alternating positive and negative ions
Separate groups of atoms joined by shared electrons
A regular lattice of atoms each joined to four others by covalent bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: A regular lattice of alternating positive and negative ions
questions.explanation: Alternating positive and negative ions in a lattice is ionic. Positive ions in delocalised electrons is metallic; the others describe covalent substances.

questions.question: A student says 'The formula NaCl shows that sodium chloride is made of molecules containing one sodium and one chlorine atom.' What is the best correction?
options: NaCl shows one Na⁺ ion bonded only to one Cl⁻ ion.
NaCl shows the ratio of ions in a giant lattice; there are no molecules.
NaCl shows the compound is covalent.
NaCl means there are two atoms in each unit cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: NaCl shows the ratio of ions in a giant lattice; there are no molecules.
questions.explanation: In an ionic compound the formula is the simplest ratio of ions. Each ion is attracted to many others, so there are no discrete molecules.

questions.question: A 3D space-filling model of sodium chloride is used. Which statement is a limitation of this model?
options: It shows the relative sizes of the ions.
It shows the ions are closely packed.
The ions in the middle of the structure cannot be seen.
It shows the structure in three dimensions.
markScheme: 1 mark: The ions in the middle of the structure cannot be seen.
questions.explanation: Space-filling models show sizes and packing well, but the inner ions are hidden from view.

questions.question: Describe the structure of an ionic compound.
markScheme: 1 mark: giant structure / lattice
1 mark: of (oppositely charged) ions (arranged regularly)
questions.explanation: Both the word giant (or lattice) and the idea of ions are needed.

questions.question: Name the forces that hold the ions together in sodium chloride and state between which particles they act.
markScheme: 1 mark: (strong) electrostatic forces of attraction
1 mark: between oppositely charged ions / between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
questions.explanation: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

questions.question: State one thing that a dot and cross diagram of sodium chloride shows well.
markScheme: 1 mark: how the electron is transferred / where electrons come from / the charges on the ions / that ions have full outer shells
questions.explanation: Dot and cross diagrams are best for showing the formation of the ions.

questions.question: A diagram of an ionic compound shows 12 potassium ions and 6 oxide ions. Work out the empirical formula. Show your working.
markScheme: 1 mark: ratio 12 : 6 = 2 : 1
1 mark: K₂O
questions.explanation: Dividing by 6 gives 2 : 1. Charge check: 2 × (+1) + (−2) = 0.

questions.question: Give two limitations of using a two-dimensional diagram to represent a giant ionic lattice.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: shows only one layer / does not show the 3D arrangement; shows only a small part of the lattice; does not show the forces / bonds; may not show relative sizes or close packing
questions.explanation: A flat diagram cannot show the arrangement above and below a layer, and shows only a few of the billions of ions.

questions.question: Explain why each sodium ion in sodium chloride is described as being held by many ionic bonds, not just one.
acceptedAnswers: attracted to all surrounding chloride ions
markScheme: 1 mark: each Na⁺ is surrounded by (six) Cl⁻ ions
1 mark: electrostatic forces act in all directions, so it is attracted to all of them
questions.explanation: The attraction is not a link between two particles only; it acts on every nearby oppositely charged ion.

questions.question: Explain why ions of the same charge are not placed next to each other in an ionic lattice.
markScheme: 1 mark: like charges repel / ions of the same charge would repel each other
questions.explanation: The lattice arrangement maximises attraction between opposite charges and keeps like charges apart.

questions.question: Compare a ball and stick model and a 3D space-filling model of sodium chloride. Give one advantage of each and one limitation of each.
markScheme: 1 mark: ball and stick: clearly shows the 3D arrangement / positions of the ions
1 mark: ball and stick limitation: sticks are not real bonds / gaps between ions exaggerated
1 mark: space-filling: shows relative sizes and close packing, but cannot see inner ions
questions.explanation: Each model shows something different; a good answer gives a specific advantage and a specific limitation for each.

questions.question: An ionic compound contains M³⁺ ions and X²⁻ ions. A diagram of a section of its lattice shows 4 M³⁺ ions. How many X²⁻ ions should it show, and what is the empirical formula?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6 X²⁻ ions (4 × 3 = 12 positive charges = 6 × 2 negative charges)
1 mark: M₂X₃
questions.explanation: Total positive charge is 12+, which needs six 2− ions. Ratio 4 : 6 simplifies to 2 : 3.

questions.question: A diagram shows a regular arrangement of particles labelled Li⁺ and F⁻. Deduce the type of bonding and the empirical formula.
markScheme: 1 mark: ionic (particles are oppositely charged ions in a lattice)
1 mark: LiF
questions.explanation: Charged particles in a lattice show ionic bonding. Li⁺ and F⁻ have equal and opposite charges, so the ratio is 1 : 1.

questions.question: Explain why sodium chloride is described as a giant structure.
markScheme: 1 mark: it contains a very large number of ions in a lattice that repeats in all directions
questions.explanation: Giant means it is not a small molecule: the pattern repeats over billions of ions.

questions.question: In the three-dimensional structure of sodium chloride, how many chloride ions are nearest neighbours of each sodium ion?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6
questions.explanation: Each Na⁺ has a Cl⁻ above, below, left, right, in front and behind: 6 in total. In a single 2D layer you only see 4.

questions.question: A diagram of part of a lattice shows 9 Mg²⁺ ions. The compound is magnesium chloride. How many Cl⁻ ions should be shown to keep the same ratio as the empirical formula?
markScheme: 1 mark: 18
questions.explanation: MgCl₂ has a 1 : 2 ratio, so 9 Mg²⁺ ions need 18 Cl⁻ ions (9 × 2 = 18).

questions.question: A model of part of a lattice of sodium oxide contains 24 ions in total. How many of these are sodium ions?
markScheme: 1 mark: ratio Na⁺ : O²⁻ = 2 : 1 (Na₂O)
questions.explanation: In Na₂O there are 3 ions per formula unit, 2 of them Na⁺. 24 ÷ 3 = 8 formula units, so 8 × 2 = 16 Na⁺ ions (and 8 O²⁻).

questions.question: A cube-shaped section of a sodium chloride ball and stick model has 3 ions along each edge. How many ions are in this section in total?
questions.explanation: A 3 × 3 × 3 cube contains 27 ions (14 of one type and 13 of the other). It is still only a tiny part of the real lattice.

questions.question: Describe the structure of sodium chloride and explain what holds it together.
markScheme: Indicative content: giant ionic lattice; regular, repeating 3D (cubic) arrangement; sodium ions (Na⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻); each Na⁺ surrounded by Cl⁻ ions (six) and each Cl⁻ by Na⁺ ions; equal numbers of each so formula NaCl; strong electrostatic forces of attraction; between oppositely charged ions; acting in all directions; very large number of ions / no molecules.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of the lattice arrangement and a correct explanation of the strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'made of ions' or 'held by ionic bonds' with limited detail
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses the key phrases giant ionic lattice and strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions, in all directions.

questions.question:
Chemists use dot and cross diagrams, ball and stick models, two-dimensional diagrams and three-dimensional space-filling models to represent sodium chloride.
Evaluate these four ways of representing sodium chloride.
markScheme: Indicative content: dot and cross: shows electron transfer and charges / full outer shells; does not show lattice arrangement, sizes, or giant structure; may suggest separate NaCl pairs. Ball and stick: shows 3D arrangement and that each ion is surrounded by opposite ions; sticks are not real bonds, forces act in all directions; large gaps between ions exaggerated; may not show relative sizes. 2D diagram: shows alternating pattern simply; only one layer; not 3D. 3D space-filling: shows relative sizes and close packing; inner ions hidden; arrangement hard to see. All: only show a small part of a giant lattice; do not show the forces. Judgement: each is useful for a different purpose, e.g. dot and cross for formation, ball and stick for arrangement.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a balanced evaluation of all four representations, with a strength and a limitation for each, and a justified conclusion
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): strengths and limitations given for some representations, or limitations only for most
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two simple points about one or two representations
questions.explanation: Evaluate means give strengths and limitations and reach a judgement. The best answers recognise that each model is chosen for a particular purpose and that none shows the whole giant lattice.
